utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: One follow-up question, General Milovanovic, before we move on today from yesterday. You told us about how on May 12th communications systems were being worked on and how they worked a bit. What I wanted to ask you is: At any time during the war, were the communications systems of the VRS knocked out and had to be -- and communications had to be used by a back-up system? And I'm referring to, I believe, around August 1995. If you could tell us if there was a communications problem at that time.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sometime around the 29th or 30th of August, 1995, the NATO Pact launched Tomahawk rockets and destroyed all of our 13 nodes, communications nodes. We were down with no communications for two hours, and in those two hours we managed to establish a back-up system. At the beginning of the war we managed to obtain four sets of communications systems. We actually had the communications system of the former staff of the -- the defence staff of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was the first set. The second set was the set that we inherited from the former military district in Sarajevo and we seized two sets, or rather, we did not let them be returned to Yugoslavia. This was the communications system of the -- the communications brigade of the Supreme Command. We only let the soldiers and -- with their side-arms leave the territory, but we kept the equipment. So we had four sets. One of those sets was operational, the other one was a back-up system, one of them was always being serviced. We had a factory called Rudi Cajavec in Banja Luka which maintained these communications systems. And there was a set that was sometimes had to be re-fitted or adapted. And as far as I can recall, we were hit by NATO Pact on six occasions and they never managed, other than this 30th or 31st of August, I can't remember, to destroy all of our 13 communications nodes so that at that point in time we were without a communications system for two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, before we move on, this question for the Defence. Mr. Robinson, the Chamber is seized of the Prosecution's request for extension of time to comply with the Trial Chamber's order compelling inspection of items material to the Sarajevo defence case which was filed yesterday. If my memory is correct, the Prosecution is suggesting disclosing some of 130 prospective witness materials by 2nd of March and then disclosing the remainder on a rolling basis by 9th of May. So if I can hear your observation on this some --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we don't object to that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the Prosecution's request is granted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, General Milovanovic. Just to move on then to make sure I understand clearly. Those two hours in August 1995, that was the only time that the communications were down during the war?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. I'm going to move on to a new topic now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That refers to military communication, General Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, military communications, command communications, command and co-ordination communications, that's what we called them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to a new topic now about -- and show you some documents and orders. And the first one is an exhibit already, P00846. Now, this document, General --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It may need to be made larger for the General, please. Perhaps, if necessary, just have the Serbian on the screen, I don't know, or split it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is an order from the president of 7 February 1994, regarding artillery use, and we see here what the president is ordering. Before I ask you anything substantive about this, do you remember seeing this document before, General?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me just to see what the order actually is. Yes, I had occasion to see this document during the war and I also saw it during one of the first interviews that were conducted with me by Mr. Barry Hogan in Banja Luka, the 23rd, 24th, and 25th of May, 2001. This is the ratio of responding to fire, where the ratio should be 1:1. If I can just see the date, please. Thank you. This is the 7th of February, 1994, in preparation of the delegation of the VRS for negotiations in Sarajevo with UNPROFOR and the Muslims on pulling out artillery to a zone 20 kilometres away from Sarajevo, and I headed the VRS delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me show you another document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is 65 ter 15598, also dated 7th of February. And if we can blow that up so that the witness can see his name at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see the signature; however, the document is very smudged and -- just a minute, please. Could we scroll it down. Thank you. I have read it. This is a document that I drafted and it is the implementation of a previous order received from the supreme commander on being careful with ammunition, or rather, responding to enemy fire one on one, in other words, a missile for a missile or a projectile for a projectile. There is a term mentioned here, shelling, and in the course of the war this term, shelling, was in fact imposed by the UNPROFOR and it's become commonplace. However, it's incorrect. In artillery, technically speaking it should be called counter-batting. In other words, you open fire on a weapon or a piece of artillery that is opening fire at you. Now, the shelling, the term "shelling," is problematic because it implies the dispersion of shells beyond the target itself, and this was never actually the case on either our side or the Muslim side. And also, there is mention here of the corps artillery group and the responsibility for it is the direct responsibility of the corps commander, whereas the deployment of artillery was in the remit of the brigade commander. In other words, if there should be a disproportionate response to enemy fire, I don't have to go looking for who was responsible; the responsibility is with the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And just then, this is, as you say, your implementing the order on the same day it was received at the Main Staff from the president?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4493, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could we see the previous document, i.e., Exhibit P846. If we could blow it up a bit further. General Milovanovic, how should we read item number 3, Corps commanders shall answer directly to the president?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The corps commander shall answer directly to me for the acts of the corps while brigade commanders shall answer for the acts of the brigades. In explaining the earlier document I stressed these two matters. Because the corps has its own artillery group for their engagement - and these are mostly large-calibre weapons and long-range weapons - whereas the brigade is 122-millimetre calibres up to 18 kilometres. In other words, the commander of the brigade is responsible for the brigade weapons. So the corps commander does not care who it was who actually fired that shell or who the platoon commander was. All he wants to know is whether it was the corps group or the brigade artillery that acted, and then they would lay the responsibility at the hands of the corps commander or the brigade commander, depending on who opened fire. So I only -- in this order, I only actually conveyed who was responsible to the Commander-in-Chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question was rather: The president was exercising command and control over those corps and brigade commanders directly by this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct. That is the power of the supreme commander, and he addressed this order - as we can see if we scroll it down a bit - to the Main Staff I believe, the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and all brigade commanders. In other words, he wanted this to reach the units as soon as possible, but he did not bypass the Main Staff. And based on that order I also had to forward this order to the Main Staff so that the brigade commander would not actually carry out orders to the third superior, but rather the orders of the Main Staff. I think, or rather, I'm certain that all this means is that the -- this commander's concept had to reach the -- those who are to implement it as soon as possible. So there is nothing unlawful in this. It would have been unlawful had the supreme commander skipped or overlooked the Main Staff when issuing this order, but he did not bypass it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: However, when you issued the implementation order, you didn't include this item, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I did and I have explained why corps commanders were responsible or what they were responsible for and what the brigade commanders were responsible for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Directly answerable to the president?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the president and to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go back to General Milovanovic's document to see it again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's for you to take up the issue in your cross-examination. Please continue, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I now have P03041. This is a document dated 31st of March, 1994, from the Main Staff marked "urgent." And, Your Honours, if there's no objection, I have a hard copy in the Serbian language which may be easier for General Milovanovic to read if he wants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Robinson? That will be done.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could scroll up a bit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Can we have a copy for us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's from -- you can see it in e-court. That's for the convenience of the General so that he can read in hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, this has been released --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can print out from the e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't need a hard copy. I can see it quite clearly on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, then.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we scroll up. Let's move on with the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to go through the whole thing now, General, because there's a particular part I wanted to ask you about. If we could go to the last page so you can see who this document came from at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I sent the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, this is quite a lengthy analysis, and I won't go through all the different paragraphs. What I wanted to focus on was the actual order, if we go to the previous page in Serbian. And this is a document, if you remember, General, that you and I looked at when we met about three weeks ago. If you could just read through the order and my question will be about section (G), the last at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we scroll up, please. That's good.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll just read it out. "(G) The commanders of corps and brigades can receive assignments and orders only from the Main Staff of the VRS and the supreme commander of Republika Srpska armed forces Dr. Radovan Karadzic and from nobody else. Before the acknowledging of orders, the commanders are obliged to report that they have received them so the superior headquarters can adjust the strategic, operational, and tactical objectives with the situation at battle-fields ..." And then I won't read it all but it continues that you strictly forbid local governing orders, Assemblies, municipal, and other bodies from giving orders --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably we need to change the next page for B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you let me know what the question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. I was just waiting for you to finish reading it. The question is: Can you explain to us why you included this order at the bottom, (G), that we've just seen, that only the Main Staff and the president can issue orders and nobody else?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is another attempt to avoid dual or parallel command system when it came to using the combat units of the VRS, although we had eliminated Crisis Staffs from the system of command. Nevertheless, these municipal organs maintained the brigades that had been established in the territory of the municipalities, and in a certain sense they considered that they had certain rights since they were feeding and maintaining the troops, they had certain rights to use the troops too. That's what they believed. The supreme commander was with the Main Staff. I told you about the event when, in front of me, he eliminated from a system of command Dusko Kornjaca, he removed him from the system of command, Dusko Kornjaca, Cajnice, and Ratko Radic at Hadzici. We took advantage of this and then got rid of all the Crisis Staffs. As far as this document itself is concerned, it has a certain background history. On the 19th of March of this year, 10 or 12 days before the document was issued, there was a briefing in the Main Staff, an assessment of the situation. This was my task, to give suggestions to the commander and to assess the situation. I thought that there would be a Muslim-Croat offensive in the spring of 1994, and I warned the Main Staff of this and mentioned all the axes that are referred to in the introduction of the order. The first time we were together, General Mladic didn't accept my assessment and my suggestions. He interrupted the briefing, and on the following day he came to see me in my office. He was on his own. He told me we would not continue with the briefing and that he didn't agree with my assessment. He said I had overestimated the enemy, that the enemy didn't have the material possibility for carrying out such a large-scale offensive. He only authorised some of my suggestions, and that was to carry out a planned action, Zvijezda 94 in the vicinity of Gorazde. And as for everything else, that was to wait for better times. On one occasion - I cannot now remember the date - but from the 20th or between the 20th and the 30th of March, I informed the supreme commander that the commander hadn't accepted my assessment. The supreme commander did not react either positively or negatively. He just said that these are your affairs in the Main Staff. On the 24th, there was an accident. Mladic lost his daughter. There was an incident. He went to the funeral in Belgrade, and that is why I signed this document as deputy commander. The enemy offensive commenced on several axes, in several areas, Posavina, Majevica, Gorazde, and I don't know, in Bugojno, in both Vakufs, and so on. And then I made good use of my assessment of the 19th of March, and I warned the corps commanders of the things that we have read about in the introduction to the order. And I also used my prerogative to issue an order for the VRS to prepare itself to mount a defence against the spring-time offensive in Bosnia and Herzegovina launched by the Muslim and Croat forces. And this is my explanation as to the provenance of this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Very quickly, 13899, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: While it's coming up, this is from the next day, 1st of April, 1994. It's an IBK, or Eastern Bosnian Corps, command document from General Novica Simic. And take a look at the cover page, General, and then we'll look at the last page. And I'm simply going to ask you if what we see is your order and the analysis being passed down to the corps. And then we see that General Simic says that all corps members shall be informed about the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So maybe we could go to the last page of the Serbian now. Perhaps one page back, sorry, so that we can see that this is the section which is the order. And then down some more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: There we see ...

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen it. What's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The question is simply: Is this the order we just looked at signed by you being passed down to the corps level, again an implementation?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is General Simic's reaction to the order of mine that we have had a look at. He didn't amend it but passed it down as it was to his subordinate units, so he was implementing the order of mine that we have just had a look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I admit -- tender this, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4494, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to jump ahead a little bit, General, and now show you some more documents. These are from March 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 07526, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is an order from President Karadzic to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, as well as to the minister of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republika Srpska, 29 March 1995. And it states in paragraph 1: "Based on RDB state security information on the intentions of the Muslims of Srebrenica to transfer 1500 manoeuvre brigade soldiers to Kladanj and previous intelligence information concerning their intentions to cut off the Vlasenica-Zvornik road, set up ambushes immediately along the possible axis of withdrawal of units and increase the number of patrols controlling the area. "2. Inform me of the execution of this order in a timely fashion." Now, the question is: You explained to us yesterday about how as president Dr. Radovan Karadzic was supreme commander of the armed forces of the RS, which included the MUP, the police, as well as the army and also civilian protection. Do you recall this order coming into the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember it. This is a typical, regular act by the supreme commander. He's forwarding the order to the troops and the Ministry of the Interior, to the police. He's sending them the order. He is warning us what might happen. I don't want to comment on the contents of the text. 1.500 soldiers, a brigade, is mentioned. The Muslims want to transfer them from the Srebrenica enclave. That is supposed to be a safe area and there should be no armed soldiers there. Soldiers are being sent from the enclave to Kladanj, to assist in the defence of Kladanj. At the time I think that we were carrying out the Krivaja 94 offensive and our objective was to take Prevoj -- the Sokolina pass between Zvornik and Kladanj. Let's put it that way. We succeeded in doing this. However, I and Milenko Karisik, I believe, the commander of the special police units, that's the combat part of the MUP, we reached an agreement, made a plan to have mixed patrols. We patrolled along the Han Pijesak-Milici-Zvornik axis and the Han Pijesak-Vlasenica-Sekovici axis. This was a matter of taking precautions, to make sure that Muslims didn't make any attempts and if they did make any attempts, for those patrols to discover them and to attack them. Another problem is mentioned here. You can't see it, but it's something you can read in between the lines. UNPROFOR knew that there were armed men in the Srebrenica enclave, and throughout that period of time these people were trying to join up with Tuzla, Kladanj, and Olovo. They wanted the Srebrenica and Zepa enclave to join up over the Susica mountain. And the VRS spent about two and a half years of the war fighting against those groups that would come out of Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender this, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be Exhibit P4495.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you talked about meeting with Mr. Karisik and I'm going to show a couple more documents related to this order from the president, some of which talk about that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have P02253, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is a 30th of March - in other words, the next day - order from the VRS Main Staff. It's to the Drina Corps command and it's about the prevention of transfer of Muslim forces from Srebrenica to Kladanj, and then we see the order. And again, before General Milovanovic -- well, I'll just tell you, General, when you get to the last page of this, page 2, you'll see that it's written by you at the bottom of the page. Now, the question is quite simple. Take a look at the document. This order emanates from the presidential order we saw the day before; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if we can go down to the time-stamp at the bottom on the right. It's not completely easy to read, at least for me, but we can see that this was received and processed at approximately 5 p.m.; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 30th of March, 5 -- or 1700 hours processed, which means that it was received at the Drina Corps command. And it was sent at 4.10 p.m., or 1610 hours, which means that it took about 40 minutes for the encryption officer to dis-encrypt it and to forward it to the commander. So this is just a military implementation of the previous order of the supreme commander, and there should be a similar document from the Ministry of the Interior and I believe we've had occasion to see it during the proofing sessions. So this is just the implementation of the supreme commander's order, and you can see here that I also ordered that a group should be sent to assist the -- this task force, and that's a group of 30 men highly trained, and they can assist very rapidly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we look at paragraph 3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a minor correction. According to the English translation, 1610 says -- means telegram number and the first line says it was received 1655. So I don't read how we can know that it took 40 minutes to decode this telegram. It was received 1655 and processed 1700. That's what it says. Do you confirm that, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we're both correct. This telegram was received at 1655. This is a telegram that was sent via teleprinter - in other words, it was encrypted - and it was completed at 1655, the decoding was completed at 1655, and its re-typing. And there's a code-name and then something is smudged. And then the 1610, that's probably the time when it was sent from my teleprinter to the Drina Corps teleprinter, and the encryption officers finally processed this at 5.00, at 1700 hours. So it took him about five minutes to re-type this. I don't see that there is anything in dispute here. This is just a technical matter. I handed this document to my teleprinter officer, he had to encrypt it, and then use the Morse code or whatever - I'm not very good with technology. But it took about 50 minutes to an hour for this telegram to actually come to the desk of the corps commander, in other words, the end user.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I think you've already explained it, General, but paragraph 3 we see here says: "By agreement with the authorised representatives of the RS MUP ensure control of the territory ..." et cetera, this task of blocking Muslim troops. Does that refer to what you just spoke about, your meeting with Milenko Karisik?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am here instructing the corps commander -- command to get in touch with the police of that region, Vlasenica, Zvornik, and the surrounding places, towns, Han Pijesak, and to co-ordinate the details regarding these mixed patrols, whatever they agree. In some cases there would be purely military patrols, in others purely police, and then there would be mixed ones. In other words, the details on the transfer of these Muslim soldiers are left to the corps commander to work out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could now have another document, again in this chain, again it's related, General. It's number 07853. We'll just take a minute to look at that one, General, sir. It's also in your name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we can continue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can we scroll down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to take a look at these stamps as well. This is from the Main Staff of the VRS, same day, 30 March 1995, very urgent. Now, this one is to the president of Republika Srpska, the supreme commander, CC: Minister of the Interior of Republika Srpska, if we go back to the top. And on the top right we have a stamp which in my translation reads: "RS president's office, 30 March 1995." Time 1750 hours. And you are responding to the president. It begins: "Re: Your order strictly confidential number 01-574/95 ..." And then it says -- and then it talks about other orders and the Drina Corps forces being engaged in Spreca 95. And I'm interested most at the moment in paragraph 3. "Ministry of the Interior of RS informed me in its letter ..." I won't read out the number "... of 23 March 1995 that some members of the PJP," special police unit, "had been based in the area of Konjevic Polje and given the task of controlling the areas of Konjevic Polje, Cerska, Udrc, and Glogova and securing the roads in this area. "We propose that the MUP forces through ambushes and patrols ensure the control of the territory in depth along the Srebrenica-Han Pogled-Kladanj axis which would, together with our intensified security and alertness along the line of contact, block this and the announced movement of the Muslim brigade from Srebrenica." And then below there we see another time-stamp, 1630, 1645 processed. So can you explain this document to us. We saw the order received from the president, the order conveyed to the Drina Corps, and this one now, can you explain what you're doing making a proposal to the president?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my report to the supreme commander that I've acted upon his order. The request to the supreme commander in paragraph 2, because of the engagement of the Drina Corps in Operation Spreca and so on, and then I say what it is that I am unable to do. And then I tell him who would be able to carry that out, and that is the MUP forces. Simply put, this is a report to the supreme commander, informing him that we have acted on his order. And in the signature block I see that I've signed this as the Chief of Staff, whereas earlier I signed the other document as the deputy commander of the Main Staff. And the reason is that I received this order from the supreme commander as the deputy commander, because Mladic was not there. He probably had returned to Bosnia in the meantime, but because I was the person who had received the first order I had to report to the supreme commander what it was that I had done. As for these stamps saying "received" and "processed," I don't see why you insist on it so much. As you can see here, this telegram was processed in 15 minutes, whereas in the upper right corner we see that it says that it was processed at 1750; in other words, an hour and five minutes were necessary for the administration of the president of the republic to log this in the main register, to put it in protocols, and then to disseminate it through his counsellors. So simply, what we see here is the way these documents, the process -- the way these documents were sent. Sometimes they are processed very quickly and they're sent by teleprinter, but here, from this upper stamp we can see that the administration didn't do their job properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. The reason I insist, as you put it, is exactly that, so you can help us understand the way this process worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender that, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Exhibit P4496.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could I now have P02254 also from 30th of March, 1995, a Drina Corps command document with the heading "Prevention of relocation of Muslim armed forces from Srebrenica to Kladanj." This is signed by the Drina Corps commander. We don't need to go there right now, but it's general -- it's signed by Milenko Zivanovic. And we can see the different brigades it's sent to. If we could go to page 2 of the English. I think it's okay, page 1 of the Serbian. At the top we see that Commander Zivanovic has written that: This is pursuant to the order of the president of the RS and the order of the VRS Main Staff and pursuant to the DK, Drina Corps's, command's assessment. If we now go to paragraph 11, which is on the next page of the English and it's on page 2 of the Serbian. And then we'll need to go over in a minute to the next page of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: A simple question, General. The reason I'm showing you this document is to ask you: Is this now what we see as the implementation of the president's order through the Main Staff and the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. One more document now on this topic. 65 ter 07049. This is the RS Ministry of the Interior office of the minister document, also dated 30th of March, to president of the RS, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, signed not by but for Minister Zivko Rakic. Now, does this document refer to the same order and task we saw, to block these Muslim armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but Minister Zika Rakic wasn't fair towards me as I was towards him. This document wasn't sent to me for my information, but I sent one to him. This is a report that he sent to the Supreme Command, according to which he acted in accordance with his order of March 1995. And as I have the microphone, in that first document that we analysed and related to this subject matter I mentioned that Krivaja 94 operation, but it was the Spreca 95 operation. It wasn't the Krivaja operation. I don't know how I made that slip. It was a corps operation, not a Main Staff operation. So I probably got confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Just before we move on, you may -- we saw the document a minute ago where you made the proposal to the president regarding engagement of the MUP forces. Do you recall if President Karadzic accepted your proposal or how you learned that he accepted your proposal, if he did?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand the question. Did I know whether the president accepted my suggestion or not? Was that the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. That -- you made a proposal, as we saw in the document that we began with. You proposed that the MUP forces be engaged on the Srebrenica-Han Pogled-Kladanj axis. I'm just wondering how did you find out, if you did, that that proposal had been accepted by the supreme commander?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having received a response from the president of the republic and it wasn't necessary, because there is a saying: Silence is tantamount to confirmation. So he didn't have to tell me whether he'd engage the police or not, but as to whether he did or not, it wasn't a matter of interest for me anymore because the command post there was General Mladic at the time. And perhaps he informed General Mladic. I don't know. I don't really think it's important whether he accepted my proposal or not because from the report from the corps commander or from his order to subordinate units, I can see that the Srebrenica-Han Pogled axis -- Srebrenica-Han Pogled-Kladanj axis had been closed off by police forces and that, in fact, was my proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move on now to another topic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to tender that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you for the reminder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be the next exhibit, P4497.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to another topic now, General. This is something that you discussed and testified about before, and that are -- and those are directives. The directives we've seen, like directive 4, directive 7, which we may discuss, can you just define those for us. What are directives? What is the purpose of a directive issued from the president to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In war time, directives from the Supreme Command are doctrinaire documents, military and political documents which amalgamate the tasks of the army within the framework of the current or future political events. A directive is a document that is issued by the Supreme Command. It guides the military forces and tells them how to act at present or in the future period. Usually they regulate future periods. Should I tell you something about the way in which directives are created?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, please, General.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Supreme Command as a military and political organ responsible for conducting war in a given country -- well, war is too serious for generals to be in charge of it. Politics has to get involved. The politicians carry out wars. If the Supreme Command had certain assessments according to which something might happen, and perhaps I incited them in my order to have such an assessment, on such occasions the supreme commander issues a task to the operations officer from the Supreme Command Staff or from the Ministry of Defence. The task consists of guide-lines. It mentions what the Supreme Command wants, what the army has to do, what the police have to do, what the civilian protection have to do. So these are the various parts that are concerned. The guide-lines don't have to be provided in written form. The operations officer can be called in, the one who is going to work on the directive, and he can be provided with the necessary oral information. Yesterday, we spoke about the fact that our Ministry of Defence wasn't capable of conducting military operations. It had no staff; that's well known. So many segments from the Ministry of Defence are segments that the Supreme Command made the Main Staff responsible for. For example, mobilisation, drafting combat documents, and so on and so forth. Later I found out that General Mladic had the task for the Main Staff to issue a directive with those guide-lines. He designated my deputy, the chief of the operations administration, General Miletic. I don't know what sort of form Miletic received those guide-lines from Karadzic in, whether it was conveyed to him orally or in written form, and he was the author of the text of directive number 7. I was the author of directive number 4 that was issued three days earlier, on the 19th of November, 1992. The other one was issued at some time around the beginning of March 1995. I don't know how Miletic created it, but I know the procedure when he produced the first version or handwritten version, as they said at the time, then it would be sent to the supreme commander for the implementation of the directive. It was so that it could be examined and so that a final form could be given to it. When the supreme commander carried out his work, he would return the directive to the author, to General Miletic, so that it could be amended. Then the final form would be given to it, it would be typed out, and he would then send it to the supreme commander so that the supreme commander could sign it. In military terms, if you have a combat document, an order or a directive, there are three individuals who are responsible for the document to have the right form: The author; the technical -- or the technician who typed it out, put it down on paper in some other way; and you have the most responsible person, and that is the person who signed the document. This should have been the way in which directive number 7 was created. What happened in the meantime after the first checks had been carried out of the draft directive, well, I don't know. Did the supreme commander make certain amendments with regard to the final version that was sent to him for him to sign. In part of the indictment against General Miletic, I had the opportunity of reading that directive, but that was ten years later, ten years after the end of the war. That much about the process that is involved when producing a directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Nicholls. You mentioned that there are three individuals who are responsible for the document in military terms. Author and signatory. Who else did you refer to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The typist, so this technical individual, if you will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you for describing the process. Could I have -- let's go right to directive 7, P00838. Now, first, General, sir, do you see that this is, in fact, what we have before us, directive 7?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go to the last page of the Serbian, which for some reason is the first page of the English. If we can go to the last page of the Serbian version -- sorry, second-to-last. And blow that up for the General to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Tell me when you've read that page, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recognise the signature on the right under your name?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And we can see it, but what's the stamp?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. It's the Main Staff's stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And this is headed "very urgent." Main Staff of the VRS. Directive for operations to the command of the 1KK, I should say 1st Krajina Corps. "Enclosed with this document we are sending you a directive for further operations, operation number 7. Confirm receipt of the above-mentioned directive by returning a copy." Now, can you just basically explain what your role was in forwarding this document to the 1KK?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between the 6th and 12th, at that time I was in the western part of the front, in Krupa na Uni. I returned on the 12th and this document probably -- well, not probably. This document -- or rather, the post had been prepared for the 1st Krajina Corps, and this is an additional document from me -- in fact, it's an order for the courier, who is to deliver it to Banja Luka. It's an order for him to give the document to the 1st KK commander. And you'll see that it took four days for the document to be delivered. He left on the 17th and confirmation from the 1st KK that it was received is dated the 21st of March. So my -- all I had to do was to see the title of the document that was being sent, and I had to attach this order to the document, this order for the courier, so that he could deliver it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you read the document at that time, in March 1995, if you remember? And by "the document," I mean directive 7.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you when I read it. I read it about ten years after the end of the war at one of these conversations or interviews, depending on how you want to call it. I was shown this along with part of the indictment that had been brought against General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you a couple questions about this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General Milovanovic, one may find it difficult to understand that you didn't read this document, directive, at the time when signing off to the subordinate corps. Could you expand on that a bit further.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This additional document is signed by the most senior officer in the Main Staff who is there when the post is being delivered to subordinates or to superiors. And probably on the 17th I was the most senior officer in the Main Staff, as a result of which I had to sign this additional document for the courier, or this cover letter. The number of the additional document isn't mine. My number is 02. The number here is 03. That is the operations administration's number. So the person who prepared the post was General Miletic. Slash 4, I can't remember exactly what his number was because they all had their own numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, this is -- as you say, you testified about this directive before. If you had read it at the time, in March 1995, would you have been able to change anything in it? Would you have been able to alter or amend the directive?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was signed by the supreme commander, the Main Staff commander received it, General Mladic. He started acting on it. You can see that the original was sent to the 1st Corps command. He probably sent it to all other corps too. Why did Mladic send the original of Karadzic's directive to subordinate units instead of only sending his combat order that was a result of the directive? I know that that order 7/1 also existed. Well, in the course of the testimony I saw that Mladic's combat order was somewhat changed in comparison with Mr. Karadzic's directive. No one could do anything with regard to the directive after the supreme commander had signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Well, that brings me just to another question which I think you've basically just answered, but it also came up when you testified before. This was drafted by Main Staff Colonel Radivoje Miletic. Could he have altered the directive, added language, taken out language, changed language, after it had been signed by President Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he couldn't do anything after Karadzic had signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to look now at page 10 in the English, 15 in the Serbian. And the part I'm focusing on, I'm sorry, is the section of where it says "Drina Corps" in the heading. Take a moment to read the tasks to the -- or what it says under the Drina Corps heading, General, and I'll ask you again, as you said you have gone through this before, I'll ask you the question: The parts of this directive which start with the words "the Drina Corps," are these tasks or duties assigned to the Drina Corps by the signatory, President Karadzic, as supreme commander?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I see the heading of this document. I don't know its provenance. Because I cannot determine from the text itself who it is who is issuing the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go to the first page again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is the directive 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could we go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we show one page -- one by one all the pages, go through the pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that the General can --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- thank you, Your Honour, for the suggestion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I've seen the heading. This is a document dated the 8th of March, 1995, from the Supreme Command of the Army of Republika Srpska, and it's directive 7, the directive from the Supreme Command. Now can we move on to the signature part, signature block.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Page 21, please, in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Processed or produced by Radivoje Miletic -- Colonel Radivoje Miletic, typed up by Spasoje Zelkovic, sergeant, and typed up in two copies. All -- and signed by Dr. Radovan Karadzic. All I can say regarding this document is why the Supreme Command sent this directive directly to the corps. I didn't see in the heading whether it had also been sent to the Main Staff, but as you can see it was typed up in two copies. In other words, one copy was to remain in the files of the Supreme Command, whereas the other copy was to be sent to the implementer, in other words, the Main Staff. So automatically this would mean that typed up in two copies is incorrect, or the other possibility is that Miletic typed this up in two copies, kept one copy for himself at the archives of the Main Staff, and the original to the Supreme Command for signature. I don't know who added these words "typed up in two copies," because it's obvious, it's evident that it could not be in two copies because it was sent to all the six corps and then to the air force and anti-aircraft defence and so on. So there would have had to be some eight copies or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. There would have been more copies. But in any event, you found a copy at the Main Staff when you returned and forwarded it to the 1KK. That's what I understood you to say.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is so. However, now that I see this stamp, there is another thing that's perplexing. We see that over the signature of the supreme commander there is a stamp of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska - in other words, it's not the Supreme Command stamp. And I really can't see how it would have been done, how it was possible for the stamp of the Main Staff to be placed over the signature of the supreme commander. So, looking at this document and at who signed it and who counter-signed it, this document is not legal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let's see the first line under number 7. "The command post of the Supreme Command shall be in the Pale area, and the KM and the PKM of the VRS Main Staff shall be in the Han Pijesak area ..." And then it talks about communications and reporting. Is that indicating that the command indicated for this directive is in Pale?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command post of the Supreme Command in the area of Pale. It was there throughout the war. In other words, he is informing the subordinates that it's not moving away from Pale. The command post and the rear command post of the Main Staff in the Han Pijesak area, those two command posts were in Han Pijesak throughout the war. In other words, he's informing those who were to implement this, that that command too is staying put, it's not moving away from where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. Now if we could go to page 10 of the English, page 15 of the Serbian, under the heading of "Drina Corps," you haven't answered my question yet which I asked you a little while ago and then you wanted to look through the document. This is something you've testified about before. Under the words "Drina Corps," which you've read through, are these tasks or duties being assigned to the Drina Corps by the supreme commander?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from reading this, the supreme commander only reiterated or supported the task assigned to the Drina Corps by the Main Staff at the time when it was established. The enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa, the protected areas, were established subsequently, and the Drina Corps then had this additional assignment, to prevent the link-up of those two enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa and their link-up with Gorazde. And then there was the other order that we saw about the manoeuvre and the transfer of the Muslim forces from -- between Srebrenica and Kladanj. These were permanent tasks of the Drina Corps, they were ongoing tasks. Now, here I see that the supreme commander is envisaging another operation, Operation Zvijezda, but not 94 anymore, it's 95. The Operation Zvijezda 94 Gorazde was limited to a protected area within a perimeter of 3 kilometres; and here I see that he's ordering the Drina Corps, or rather, the Army of Republika Srpska that Operation Zvijezda 95 is to return the Muslim army back into this 3-kilometre area. I don't see anything out of the ordinary here. However, this directive is too detailed for the Supreme Command to have produced it because it provides or it issues assignments to units two levels below the Supreme Command. So it should have been forwarded to the Main Staff for it to then work it out the way it is presented here. It was probably considered that because Colonel Miletic was the one who processed this document, that it was, in fact, thereby produced by the main command.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last sentence, General. The interpreters didn't hear your last sentence, after you referred to Colonel Miletic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is possible that the supreme commander considered that this was a joint document of the Main Staff and the Supreme Command because the author of the document was a member of the Main Staff. And so he would have given details for these various assignments to units because there is a gap here of two levels of command. The Main Staff was bypassed and the next level was the commander of the subordinate unit, and that was not really necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: But, General, can you assist us, please, with the last sentence of that paragraph headed "Drina Corps." "By planned and well-thought-out combat operations create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." Would this have been part of the task assigned to the Drina Corps by the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This task was assigned to the Drina Corps directly by the Supreme Command. As far as I can recall from my earlier testimonies, when we looked at Mladic's order, sentences of this nature were non-existent. There was no reference to the population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Are we breaking or continuing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I note the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, we will need to intervene in the transcript. On page 22, line 9, where General Milovanovic said that the directive was a doctrinary document, which did not make it into the transcript, up until this line -- let me see what line that is, where General Milovanovic said that following the directive as a general document, General Mladic would then produce an executive order as directive 7.1. In other words, it is not shown in the transcript that after the directive General Mladic would produce his own document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 22. In the meantime, General Milovanovic, do you confirm what Mr. Karadzic just said?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did -- if I may, Your Honour, did you say all of that exactly that way, is the question, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes -- or for the benefit of the transcript if you can tell us about that again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, as you wish. I mean, I accept and I agree, rather, with the remark made by Mr. Karadzic because that is, indeed, what I said. But I can also repeat it if you so wish. Pursuant to the directive from the Supreme Command, the Main Staff or General Mladic specifically has to develop his own combat order and define the tasks assigned to his subordinate units. And as far as I could see, he produced -- I don't know if it was an order or a directive 7.1, or rather, 7/1. So that was the first document that was produced following directive number 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take a break for half an hour and resume at ten past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you hear me, General?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good. Almost done with questions about directive 7, but I would like to show you one more document, that's P03040.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this was not on my notification. I discussed with Mr. Robinson during the break that I would be bringing it up and it's arisen a bit from the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, General, we were just discussing and Judge Baird asked you a question about tasks for the Drina Corps. What I'm showing you now is a command of the Drina Corps document dated 20th of March, 1995. It says "Copy number 9," to the commands of the various brigades, "order for defence and active combat operations number 7." And I'm not going to go through the whole document, but can we go to the last page so that we can see that it is signed by the Drina Corps commander. You can see it was drafted by Colonel Milenko Lazic. Now I'd like to go to page 5 of the English, which is page 3 of the Serbian, where we see number 2, "Tasks of the Drina Corps." Drina Corps tasks as of 20th of March, 1995. And it starts off: "Enemy breakthroughs along selected operational tactical lines should be prevented ..." et cetera. If we could go to the next page of the English, we can stay on that same page in the Serbian, and see the end of this first paragraph. And we talked just before the break about directive 7 going to the corps and the brigades. I want to look at the last sentence of that first paragraph which is being sent to all the brigades of the Drina Corps. "By planned and well-thought-out combat operations create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." So my question is simply: Having seen this, we looked at directive 7 a moment ago, what does this Drina Corps order say about whether those tasks in directive 7 that we discussed were also tasks directly for the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me to confirm the accuracy of what is written here or to give you my comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm asking for you not to confirm just the accuracy of what is written, but your comment on whether, now seeing this, what we saw under the "Drina Corps" heading in directive 7 were, in fact, tasks for the Drina Corps which were recognised as such by the Drina Corps commander in this order? This paragraph is entitled: "Tasks of the Drina Corps." That's my question: Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This sentence that you pointed out, make living conditions unbearable and so on, this is the original sentence simply copied from directive number 7 that was signed by the supreme commander. However, in this document I did not see - so can we go back to the heading - whether General Zivanovic started this document with the words: "On the basis of directive number 7 of the Supreme Command ..." or "order 7/1 of the Main Staff."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Take a look and take your time reading the heading.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an introduction. Could we please move down a bit to the part where it says: "I hereby order ..." All of this is simply copied from the order of the Supreme Command because how would the commander of the corps know what France and other countries were doing? He wanted to -- actually, can we move the text further down. Still, there's only a reference to the general situation in the theatre of war. There's a reference here to the enemy, the enemy forces' intentions, and so on. So this is still an introduction into the order itself. And this is paragraph 2, "Tasks of the Drina Corps." Again, this is copied from the directive of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How do we know --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hereby decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- that's copied from the directive, how do we know that, or the task was defined by the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that because a moment ago I saw the original directive. I saw the tasks given to the Drina Corps and I see that the sentences are identical. He didn't change anything. But now in paragraph 4 he starts out by saying, "I have decided ..." Now, I have to see whether this is Mr. Karadzic's decision or the decision of the corps commander. Please allow me to read this paragraph and then I will answer your question. Yes, this is a decision of the corps commander, that is to say, that he continues now. After this paragraph there should be paragraph 5 that would read "tasks to subordinate units."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the corps commander didn't refer to the president's directive here. He just set out the task, tasks -- could we see number 2 again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: English is page 5 and 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It says "The Tasks of the Drina Corps," so we can -- we take it that it's defined by the corps commander. It's the tasks defined by the corps commander, although it may be identical with the directive of the president. He agreed and he defined the tasks himself here again. What is your observation to such comment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would say what I see, and what I see is that he fully, in paragraph 2, copied the tasks of his corps, as had been set out to him by his supreme commander. However, there were already some bits of his own at the very end.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We could not find it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So even this order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, for the benefit of the interpreters, could you repeat what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I do apologise to the interpreters. Even this very last line - and at first I thought that it was Zivanovic's, or rather, that it was written by the corps commander - it has to do with the command post and the forward command post, that was also copied from the directive of the Supreme Command. So paragraph number 2, "Tasks of the Drina Corps," this was literally copied from directive number 7. However, a moment ago I asked to see the heading so that I can link things up. On the basis of what General Zivanovic wrote up this document, was it on the basis of directive number 7 or Mladic's order, 7/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: General, I can help you this is entitled: "Order for defence and active combat operations, operative number 7," as we see on page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: First page. Mr. Nicholls, is it your case that this operation number 7 refers to directive number 7?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Our case is that in this combat -- operative number 7 it does indeed relate directly to directive 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Without specific reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, it doesn't say "directive 7 of the supreme commander" in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And what was your question for the General?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think he answered my last question. He asked to see the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me just ask you one question, General, and I'll try to move on from this. But if we go to page 3 of the Serbian, page 7 of the English, at the bottom you said that the forward command post and rear command post was also copied direct from directive 7. Doesn't this say the KM shall be in Vlasenica, which is not what was said in directive 7?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know now what directive number 7 said. However, gentlemen, let us not torment ourselves any further. This is Zivanovic's document, and between it and directive number 7 of the Supreme Command there is a discrepancy. Mladic's directive 7/1 is not there. General Zivanovic was not supposed to use the original directive number 7. If General Mladic had altered it - and I know that he had altered it because when I first testified in the Popovic et al. case, that was mentioned, this particular sentence was referred to, every day combat operations creating conditions of total insecurity, I think, and so on. It's a bit illegible. Then we established during that testimony that in Mladic's directive number 7/1, this sentence is simply not there. And then somebody -- I don't know whether it was the Defence attorney or the Prosecutor who asked me how could that have happened? And I explained to him that Mladic deleted this sentence, took upon himself the responsibility of not carrying out the order of the supreme commander. Because his assessment was whatever it was, I don't know what his assessment was, but at any rate he thought that this sentence should not be in the strategy of using the Army of Republika Srpska. So the army was not aiming against the civilian population. Why General Zivanovic did that, well, probably out of ignorance. Let us now not give more thought to other things, although I would be entitled to do that. Maybe he wanted to pander to the supreme commander because he bestows ranks upon people and gives promotions and so on. But maybe his assessment was that this sentence did have some kind of justification; however, he disregarded the order of his immediate superior which he was not supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let --

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite simply, the document is unlawful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you remind me the date of directive 7/1, General, or Mr. Nicholls. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, directive 7/1 is 31st of March, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry? The 31st of?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: March 1995, so 11 days later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: After this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So when General Zivanovic issued this operative, 7/1 did not exist?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does it change your observation, General Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it doesn't, because when we had a look at directive 7 a minute ago, Supreme Command passed the directive number 7 down to the Main Staff and to the corps commands, so to the second subordinates, and perhaps General Zivanovic wasn't expecting Mladic's directive. So he immediately, on the basis of Karadzic's directive, wrote this document of his because in the text he doesn't refer to either of the directives. He starts immediately with a military political assessment from a directive number 7. So it was his duty. I don't know whether such a document exists, but when he received Mladic's directive 7/1, it was his duty to amend his combat order. Nowhere did I find that he did that. Or when he received Mladic's order, he believed that he had passed his order down to the units, it wasn't necessary to amend it, and this sentence reached the brigade commander, the sentence about creating intolerable conditions for the civilian population. So we have a double mistake, the mistake of the Supreme Command that was passed down to the corps command, and then the corps commander's mistake, as he acted on the basis of that directive and didn't wait for the directive of his immediate superior, but drafted his own combat order. I don't know, perhaps the Prosecution has a correction or amendment to this order of Zivanovic's, but I don't remember it. I haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you going to leave this subject?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was going to move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, then, General Zivanovic -- no, I'm sorry, Milovanovic. There's a point that I have difficulty understanding you. You just testified that the Supreme Command passed the directive number 7 down to the Main Staff and to the corps command. It may be true, but wasn't it you that sent again the directive to the corps command, as we see in the case of 1st Krajina Corps on the 17th of March?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we are both right. I sent the directive number 7 only to the 1st KK command, the 1st Krajina Corps command. I don't know why that happened, but we saw in the original directive from the Supreme Command that there were two copies that had been made and they were forwarded to the Main Staff and to all the corps commands, the air force and anti-aircraft defence. So it went to the Main Staff and to the subordinate commands, or rather, the commands that were subordinated to the Main Staff. So this is a matter of disseminating the document. It's not the personal responsibility of the supreme commander. It's the responsibility of those assisting him. So they copied the directive, made copies of it, and this was illegal. One copy of the directive should have arrived at the Main Staff, and then the Main Staff amends it or in accordance with the decision from the commander passes it down to subordinate units. So that is probably how this document of Zivanovic's was created as a result of someone acting in a rather confused and hasty manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Having seen the case of 1st Krajina Corps, can we not take it that similar -- same copy would have been sent to the Drina Corps by you, General Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what the operations officer did, Colonel Miletic, in fact. Perhaps he complained to the 1st Krajina Corps commander that he didn't receive the directive, it was only separated and sent to him and I sent -- I signed the additional document on the 8th of March, when the document was issued, up until the 17th of March, when I sent a copy to the 1st Corps, well, I don't know what happened during that period of time. I don't know whether other corps received them, because the Drina, Eastern Bosnian, and Sarajevo Corps were in the vicinity of the command post of the Main Staff. Perhaps their officers went there and took a copy directly from the Main Staff. I quite simply don't have an explanation as to why the directive only went to the 1st Krajina Corps and was delivered to that corps through a courier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: But, General, at the end of the day, are you maintaining that the combat order of General Zivanovic was not lawful?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because it relates to the original directive from the Supreme Command, not to the Main Staff directive that was created on the basis of the Supreme Command directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, General, you've told us you didn't read directive 7 at the time and read it ten years later. So what you're doing when you're explaining how all this worked with directive 7 and 7/1 is explaining how you think things worked, analysing a document in retrospect that you never read when you received it in March 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct that at the time I didn't read directive number 7. And as far as I can remember, in the course of today's testimony you asked me to comment on the directive, or rather, on the manner in which directives are created, directives in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Let me show you another document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 6 -- I think it's been exhibited now. It was 65 ter 01977. I know it's been exhibited but, I apologise, I don't have the exhibit number. That's Krivaja 95.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit 3054.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This may help, General. This is dated 2nd July 1995, command of the Drina Corps, copy number 3 of Krivaja 95. This is an order for active combat operations. If we go to the last page, you'll see that it's again signed by the Drina Corps commander, same Drina Corps commander, obviously, Milenko Zivanovic. I'd like to go to page 3 of the English, which should be page 2 of the Serbian. Now, under point 2: "The Command of the Drina Corps pursuant to Operations Directives number 7 and 7/1 of the VRS Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and on the basis of the situation in the Corps area of responsibility, has the task of carrying out offensive activities with free forces deep in the Drina Corps zone as soon as possible in order to split apart the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica and reduce them to their urban areas." Below we see "objective" at the bottom of paragraph 4. "Objective: By a surprise attack, to separate and reduce in size the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, to improve the tactical position of the forces in the depth of the area, and to create conditions for the elimination of the enclaves." And we don't need to go to the last page now, but a copy of this does go to the Main Staff. So my question is: This order from the Drina Corps commander Zivanovic does not cite just 7/1, it cites directive 7 and 7/1. Can you just explain to us why that would be the case if the only relevant directive was 7/1? If you know.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't know. On the 2nd of July, 1995, I was in Drvar. However, as I'm an expert of a kind for combat documents, well, I can say that General Zivanovic was referring to directive number 7 and directive number 7/1 as well. This isn't justified, he shouldn't have done this. He should have just referred to one of the directives. When we discussed his order that was created on the basis of directive number 7 from the Supreme Command I asked whether there was some subsequent document that modified that sentence we referred to, and here it is under paragraph 2: "The Command of the Drina Corps on the basis of directive number 7 and 7/1 ..." and then it says what it says. Directive number 7 and 7/1 differ in regard of that sentence that concerns creating impossible conditions, intolerable conditions, for the survival of the civilian population. Well, he quite simply shouldn't have referred to two documents. He's carrying out the order of his immediate superior, General Mladic, and it is for General Mladic to see how he will deal with the supreme commander because he failed to include a sentence from Mr. Karadzic's directive. So the corps commander got a little tangled up in that web. There is an expression in the Serbian language that is not quite nice. It means to want to do things both ways. He wanted to carry out the order of the supreme commander, but the commander of the Main Staff is preventing him from doing so. So he takes the language from both documents, and this is not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, I was -- I think I must have been mistaken. I was advised that this document hasn't been admitted yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In that case, I tender it, Your Honour. I thought it had been the other day --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll give a new number for this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4498, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I please have P00976.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is directive 4, General, which you're acquainted with and have talked about. Do you need to see the last page? Would you like to see the last page for your signature or your name?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not necessary. I'm familiar with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you drafted this document; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And was it approved by the supreme commander?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When this document was completed, I first informed the supreme commander about the fact we were having a different conversation that didn't concern this. I told him that directive number 4 would be arriving. I asked him to have a look at it and to sign it. The Vice-President, Koljevic, arrived at the command post of the Main Staff. Very quickly, the Supreme Command wasn't functioning then. It was the Presidency that was in function. He brought me this directive and said that the supreme commander had authorised the directive, he had approved of it. But since it was something that concerned the military structure alone, he said that General Mladic, the commander of the -- should sign the directive, which he did.
