So the supreme commander didn't sign it. The army's commander signed it, with the approval of the supreme commander. The supreme commander saw it before it was signed by Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go to page 5 of the English which, if I have it right, is page 23 in the Serbian. It's I think re-printed twice in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And again looking at Drina Corps tasks under (d). Now, General, I'm going to ask you about this sentence that you've explained before. Just for the Trial Chamber in this case, we see: "The Drina Corps from its" -- I should have said at the beginning, sorry, for the record. This is dated November 19, 1992, so we're going back in time a few years. "The Drina Corps: From its present positions, its main forces shall persistently defend Visegrad (the dam), Zvornik, and the corridor, while the rest of its forces in the wider Podrinje region shall exhaust the enemy, inflict the heaviest possible losses on him and force him to leave the Birac, Zepa, and Gorazde areas together with the Muslim population." Now, the -- inflicting the heaviest possible losses on the enemy and forcing the enemy to leave, that's clear. Can you explain why, though, it says here "together with the Muslim population"?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to say something. It's not "together with the Muslim population."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, if there are a lot of mistakes because of the translation, when am I going to correct them? It's not "together with the Muslim population." This changes the meaning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, the General has the B/C/S original in front of him. He's following the document from the original. He can comment on it. And if there's something further you can explore, you can do it in your cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, it doesn't concern the text. It concerns Mr. Nicholls' question, in which he changed the wording. He said "together with the Muslim population." That is not correct. That is not what it says in the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. General, could you read out the part which refers to the Drina Corps. Could you read it aloud for us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can. "The Drina Corps: From the present positions, where the brunt of the forces persistently defend Visegrad (the dam)," that's the hydro-electric power-plant dam of Visegrad, "Zvornik and the corridor, and the other forces are to be used in the general area of Podrinje to exhaust the enemy, inflict as many losses as possible on him, and force him to leave the area of Birac, Zepa, and Gorazde with the Muslim population. Previously offer the disarming of able-bodied men and armed men, and if they refuse, destroy them. Further deblock and repair the road: Milici-Konjevic Polje-Zvornik, and be ready for intensive combat against inserted sabotage terrorist raids -- raid groups and paramilitary groups. The command post shall be in Vlasenica and forward command post as decided by the ... commander." Is there something you want me to explain with reference to what I've just read out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That is sufficient for now. What we hear: "Force the enemy to leave areas with the Muslim population." We didn't hear "together with," but what we heard is just "with." I'll leave it in your hands to take up from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, would you have a different interpretation of that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency. It does not say here that the army should lead the population; rather, it is implied that the population want to leave themselves and in that case the army would go with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is -- I understand he was answering this, but this is now argument not translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I saw you raise your hand, General. I want to ask --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. The issue is how to properly interpret this sentence. It should be properly interpreted to reflect the spirit of the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, this directive number 4 was in evidence from a long time ago. That's -- such translation is raised in a proper manner, not when the witness is being examined by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, General, as you read out the sentence, as you read it in your language, could you explain to us why there is a reference there to the Muslim population leaving? Why is the Muslim population referred to in there?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can and I will. Because of this sentence, I was considered a suspect in 2005, because two items were mistranslated or misinterpreted in the transcript. First the word "iznuravanje." If you take a look at the transcript of 18 October 2005 in Banja Luka, the word "iznuravanje" is translated as --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Which is "attrition," interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- is translated as "izguravanje" which is "pushing out." Now, Your Honour, you were a member of the Trial Chamber when I testified in late May 2007 and you put the following question to me. When we finally -- when the Prosecutor and I finally agreed that this sentence actually means to force it to leave the area with the Muslim population, you then put -- you asked me how it was that I knew that the Muslim population would be leaving from that area. And then I tried to explain. The Prosecutor interrupted me at one point, but after an intervention by the Defence counsel, Ms. Faveau, I was allowed to explain it through the end. I said that the nations of China, France, and Serbia are well-known nations or people, populations, that move behind the army, they move with the army after them. Now, in the last war in our areas, this was something that the Muslims also started doing. As soon as there was fighting somewhere in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the population would start moving. The Serbs would flee to the areas where there was a majority of Serb population because of security reasons. The Muslims did the same, plus they also went to third countries. In other words, they were leaving the areas where there was shooting. Proof of that, for instance, on the 16th of January, 1993, when Skelani was attacked, over 20.000 Serbs crossed over the Drina River from Eastern Bosnia. I expected that the Muslims, too, once we exert armed pressure, when we exert pressure on the armed forces of the so-called BH, that the Muslims too would start moving. Our objective was to also force the army to move behind this population or to move with them, not to remain there. So my expectation was that the civilians would start moving out, and I wanted to make sure that the Muslim army did not remain there, that they too should move out. And I believe that it is well-known why it was that we did not want the Muslim army in central Podrinje. Because from May 1992 up until 14th February 1993, they destroyed 156 Serb villages and hamlets, killed over 1.300 and something Serbs. There is a cemetery in Bratunac containing 780 graves, and I first saw this cemetery in August 1992, which means that in the three months in Bratunac municipality alone, some 780 people were killed. That is the explanation for this sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't know if you had a question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to show you P02085, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And just one correction, Mr. Nicholls, while you're waiting for that document. I was advised that Krivaja 95 was admitted under different 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which was -- I was told that the number for that exhibit was P4481.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Your Honour. I'm sorry, I had a different number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, General, directive 4 was 19 November 1992. As with directive 7, I'm now going to look at the Drina Corps command document, which relates to that. This one is Drina Corps command, 24 November 1992, very urgent, "Decision for further operations, to the Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade (personally to the Commander or Chief of Staff)." And it says specifically: "Pursuant to the Directive of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska strictly confidential number 02/5 of 19 November 1992 and an assessment of the situation, I have decided: "1. Launch an attack using the main body of troops and major equipment to inflict on the enemy the highest possible losses, exhaust them, break them up or force them to surrender, and force the Muslim local population to abandon the areas of Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde." Is that what it says in the Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So how do you account for this language, which is not exactly the same but quite close to the language in directive number 4?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to me, it's not even close, the language. In directive 4 it doesn't say anywhere force the Muslim population out or expel the Muslim population. This can just be a personal view or idea of the general of this corps who then passed this down to a subordinate unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I think I'll leave that there. I'd like to change topics now, General, and move on to something we discussed when we met, and that is the 14th Session of the Supreme Command which you attended in April 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 22049, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is quite a lengthy document, so it would be impossible to go through all the sections of it. I just want to ask you about a couple parts of it and some background. First of all, just to help you remember, do you remember that we gave you a copy of this to read in Serbian when I met you a few weeks ago -- or we actually gave it to you in advance of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You gave me - sent it to Banja Luka - the minutes from a session of the Supreme Command held on the 31st of January -- I apologise, the 31st of March, 1995. It had 93 pages. And as for this document, you did not send it to me, to Banja Luka. The only document that I did get was the 31st March session document, and I received it in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let -- let --

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, if you showed me some of what it says there, I could maybe remember whether you've shown it to me here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there because you're absolutely right. Could we go to page 2 of each document. I was reading off the cover sheet here which says: State Secret, RS Office of the President of the Republic, Main Staff of Republika Srpska, personally to the Commander-in-Chief, and this is dated 5th of April from Major-General Bogdan Subotic. If we look at the next page, I think that we can see -- you're absolutely right, the session was the 31st of March, 1995, in Pale. Now that you've corrected me, do you remember that these are the minutes we gave you to review?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, there were -- this Supreme Command session went from, again, at 5.00 p.m. and ended at 2 .15 in the morning, so it was a long session. And there was several topics addressed here. Again, I won't go through all of them. But this one issue -- well, let me ask you this, I'm sorry. Let me start again. I believe this was an extraordinary session. Can you briefly, as briefly as you can, explain to us why this session was held in March 1995. Who called for it and why it was held.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have it precisely stated where it says that this is an extraordinary session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It doesn't say that. I'm basing that on my knowledge. The witness can correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, first of all, it is numbered. It was the 14th Session, in other words, it was not an extraordinary session. To be honest, I never paid much attention to the numeration of the sessions of the Supreme Command because there were many extraordinary sessions, interim sessions, and so on. Rather, I took note of the dates and times when the session was held and I linked it to the situation in the battle-ground. Now, I recall this session very well. Perhaps if you put -- if you're more specific in your questions I can answer them because this -- these minutes have 93 pages. It took me three days to read it through. In order to comment on it, I would need five times as much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. You're correct. I'll give you some precise questions. If we go to page -- the page we're on, we can see who's attending. Was this the full membership of the Supreme Command at that time? Dr. Karadzic, Nikola Koljevic, Dr. Plavsic, Mr. Krajisnik, Dusan Kozic, Milan Ninkovic, and Tomo Kovac?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let's go to page 9 of the English, pages 8, to begin with, of the Serbian. Now, there we see -- it's paragraph 11 I'm looking at in the Serbian, towards the bottom of the page, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, briefly if I summarise, above paragraph 11, General Mladic says that even as a battalion commander he had the right to promote a private and a corporal, and there seems to be a dispute over -- between General Mladic and the supreme commander, Dr. Karadzic, about promotions, who has the right to promote. Could you briefly explain what that was about.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I can. That session of the Supreme Command was convened with the objective of considering the exposé of the Main Staff about the situation in the Army of Republika Srpska. The task of this -- the task to prepare this exposé was given to the Main Staff during the analysis of combat-readiness for 1994. I think that it had to be the 29th of January, 1995, when we from the Main Staff and the directly subordinated corps commanders explained to -- complained to the supreme commander because the Army of Republika Srpska was not properly funded and equipped. Our reserves were running out for everything that was necessary for combat. From a social point of view, our officers were having a very hard life. And then the supreme commander ordered us to prepare this exposé to describe all of these troubles that the army was facing, and he said that he would take action, or rather, convene the National Assembly so that this exposé could be discussed and so that the deputies, the members of parliament, could take a position as to whether the army should be helped or not and what should be done in general. When the supreme commander left, we were given tasks according to sectors, namely, every sector in the Main Staff was supposed to describe its own problems and line of work. Specifically, my sector was given the task that it always had, that is to say, combat operations and what we expected in the future, what we expected from the enemy. The logistics sector was the busiest one, that was General Djukic's sector. He was supposed to deal with all these troubles that we were facing in dealing with the army, and that was indeed done and that is why this session on the 31st of March was convened. So we had a month to do all of that. In the meantime, the National Assembly passed a new Law on the Army of Republika Srpska, and a new Law on Defence on the Army of Republika Srpska. Before this was passed in the Assembly, these two laws were submitted to the Main Staff and the corps commands to have views accommodated, as it were. It was called a public debate. We had quite a few objections or amendments, if you will, as one says in parliamentary parlance. As for both of these laws, none of our amendments were adopted. The Assembly voted for the laws in their original version. On that 31st, when the Supreme Command session was opened, the supreme commander presented the agenda that you can see here, so I don't have to refer to it. However, for reasons unknown to me, General Mladic stated that with regard to the first item, it would not be a good thing for us to have a discussion because allegedly we had not finished the exposé. The exposé had been finished in its working version. The Supreme Command was supposed to adopt it, and then as such it would be presented to the Assembly. Then the vice-president interjected, the vice-president of the republic, who was a member of the Supreme Command, Mr. Nikola Koljevic. He asked for the following. Before the official agenda was embarked upon, he and General Gvero should report to the Assembly because during the previous few days they had toured the entire front line of Republika Srpska. Because of this intervention by Mr. Koljevic, the agenda itself was shaken. First, General Mladic objected to the Supreme Command, saying that some of his powers had been taken away from him in terms of army control and command. Actually, according to the first law, as for NCO ranks, commissioned officer ranks, and general ranks, decisions on promotion to these ranks were made by the supreme commander. As for promotion of officers to the rank of colonel, these decisions were to be made by the minister of defence. Interim promotions of all other NCOs, officers, commissioned officers, that is, up to the rank of lieutenant-colonel was under the jurisdiction of the commander of the Main Staff. This new law, or rather, the Law on the Army and on National Defence took away that right from the commander of the Main Staff. And you see here that General Mladic rebelled. He said that as a major he could promote a corporal, a lance corporal, et cetera, but according to this law he couldn't even do that. And then that discussion started. The exposé was disregarded. Members of the army, or rather, of the Main Staff, except for me, were attacked. It was said that they did not respect state organs. And now examples were being given. For example, what was held against Mladic was that he interfered in state affairs and that he was not up to that. Then he on his part always said that members of the Supreme Command, specifically Mr. Karadzic, was a walking state, and so on and so forth. So this was this kind of political squabbling. In my assessment, I was not attacked. And to tell you the truth, I felt good about that because often the Supreme Command excluded me from these attacks, if I can call them that. So it was a bit embarrassing for me within the Main Staff. It seemed that I was wearing somebody else's jersey, if you will. It seemed that I supported the Supreme Command rather than the Main Staff. I think that the supreme commander did that sometimes perhaps unconsciously because he invited me to sessions of the Supreme Command, in spite of Mr. Mladic being there. And irrespective of how Dr. Karadzic views this as a psychiatrist, this was not easy for me. The speaker of the National Assembly took the floor, he was also a member of the Supreme Command, that was Mr. Krajisnik. And he wanted to give an example that would show that I also did not honour decisions made by state organs, and then he mentioned the example that is contained in these minutes here. But, Mr. Prosecutor, I think that this will do by way of an introduction on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So one issue was, as you've discussed, promotions; another issue I believe which you may have mentioned was the logistical supply of the army and the army not being adequately equipped with equipment it needed. Is that right as well, just one of the problems at that time?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was supposed to be an item on the agenda of this session of the Supreme Command; however, because of these unimportant things, things turned in another direction, in the opposite direction. So the session did not resolve the problem for which it had been called in the first place. General Mladic and the supreme commander at the end of the session did draw certain conclusions on the basis of which it seemed that everything had been fine at that session, that we had exchanged views, reached agreement, and so on. As for depriving Mladic of this right to promote people and grant ranks to that, he defended the Supreme Command, saying that he -- or rather, the supreme commander said that he accepted all the proposals of the Main Staff relating to promotions. I personally was satisfied with that. I don't know to what extent other members of the Main Staff were satisfied, but I didn't want to state that specifically then so that it would not turn out again that I was a black sheep in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand that. Thank you. Let me now turn to the section where Mr. Krajisnik spoke and in a way -- I don't want to characterise it, but spoke about his interaction with you, and that's on page 28 of the English - that's right - and on page 25 of the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, sorry to ask. I just wonder when -- will we take the break at the normal time or go a little bit later?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, as usual, in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Then I'll just ask you now to -- if we could blow up the part just where Mr. Krajisnik speaks large enough for the witness to read it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, we spoke about this and you raised it. The part I want to ask you about is this, and it's the part about freedom of movement. "When we signed a document which allowed free passage, freedom of movement was permitted with the intention that we could pull out the greatest possible number of Serbs from the Muslim part of the territory, and if the Muslims want to go from our territory, then we enable them to leave the area, our area, without coercion because we do not have the right to do that. Nor should anyone take on himself their ethnic cleansing, but there would be no crying if they left from here. In connection with that, I was not up on who organised a convoy that went towards Okucani. An order had gone out from the Main Staff, from General Mladic, that had forbidden the passage of that convoy. Was that only for that convoy or for something else?" And then he -- I'll skip a little bit. "I made a very polite call to General Milovanovic and said, Please, General, I have received an urgent message that the convoy should leave. We have to let it go, to see to its freedom of movement. General Milovanovic told me, I cannot now interpret that whole flow of the conversation." He says that there was an order. And further down in the next paragraph, Mr. Krajisnik says: "General, we will tell you all residents have the right to leave. I was not able" -- this is now on page 26 of the Serbian. "I was not able to say relating only to the Muslims that a small percentage of them might possibly return but a large percentage would leave." So just before we -- well, maybe if we take the break now I'll ask you what that was about when you come back, General. Or we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we finish --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- this topic and take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We'll do it now, General. Thank you. Could you just please explain what was Mr. Krajisnik's complaint there? What was he complaining about that he made a call to you and this convoy hadn't been allowed out?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, in relation to what you said with regard to this topic, you said that Krajisnik wanted to explain our co-operation. It was not co-operation. It was lack of co-operation. He accused me of not co-operating with the state organs, and he supported that by this discussion that you read out here. He said that that was supporting evidence. You will see that in my response to him; however, I can make it shorter. It is correct that he was the head of the delegation or the chairman of some commission for freedom of movement within Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't know. Mr. Karadzic knows that better. It was some kind of action or drive called Blue Roads or something like that, ensuring freedom of movement. However, the Muslims were not allowed to leave Sarajevo, Srebrenica, Tuzla, and some other towns. Since we had a reserve homeland nearby, across the Drina River, our deserters and the civilian population too, as soon as there was any kind of shooting 20 kilometres away from the Drina River, they fled across the Drina. General Mladic wrote an order, or rather, signed it, stating that without his knowledge, military conscripts could not cross the front line or the state border. At the time we had a state border with Serbia, Montenegro, and Croatia. The front lines were practically internal ones, filtrating boundaries, as they're called, between the Muslim-Croat Federation, that is, in Republika Srpska. It is correct that Krajisnik did call me on one occasion and he said to me that he had been informed, or rather, that someone from Gradiska was asking him to intervene to allow four buses full of people, I think. Most of them were Muslims and a few Croats. They wanted to leave Bosnia-Herzegovina. They wanted to go to Croatia. However, that morning -- or rather, before Krajisnik, Colonel Bogojevic called me. He was an intelligence officer in the command of the 1st Krajina Corps. And he said to me that the police, our military police, had stopped the buses with these people who wanted to cross the border. I asked him, "Why did you stop them? Who organised this?" And he said, "It was privately organised, but I have orders from General Mladic, the Main Staff, that I should not allow able-bodied men of any ethnicity to cross the border." And I said, "Bogojevic" -- or actually, I called Tolimir, General Tolimir, because he was nearby in barracks, and I asked him whether he knew about that order because I probably did not remember it anymore. Tolimir came and brought me that order and he said, "You've got this order of General Mladic. This was not allowed and so on and so forth." I told him the whole story and he said, "Well, the smartest thing for you to do would be to probably stop this." I conveyed that to this colonel, that this should be halted, and I think I said to him that the buses should be returned, that they could not cross over because of that order. Soon after that, Krajisnik called me, and this is how it started first. First he sang my praises. He knew how to talk to people. He said, "General, you are the almighty in the army. You can do this, you can do that. You see, there is this collision with some order of Mladic's and I'm asking you to be reasonable, to allow these four buses to cross over." And I said that I knew about this and that Bogojevic informed me about it, and I ordered that these buses be returned because I did not want to violate Mladic's order. Again, he tried in a nice way to say, "Well, General, don't do this, don't do that. Well, you see these people have addressed me asking for my help because I signed this," whatever it was, declaration on freedom of movement in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I said to him, "General Mladic is not here at the command post now. He is the only one who can retract his order in full or partly." However, I said, "You have the supreme commander there as well who can totally annul Mladic's order." And then all hell broke loose. I am as firm as a rock, as hard as a rock. I do not need Karadzic's protection. I do not need Mladic's protection. And basically the conversation stopped there and I said that I was carrying out Mladic's order. These buses were returned. To tell you the truth, I had forgotten all about that until that session. What happened at the session happened. He launched this attack and you have in the text that follows my defence, although Tolimir sat next to me and nudged me, saying that I should react straight away. I didn't want to. But Tolimir was whispering about this process of organising this private organisation of having Muslims and Croats cross the state border. And then I answered verbatim what it says in the text that follows, in the minutes, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a break for an hour and resume at 1.35. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.37 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could just take one moment to address very quickly some scheduling matters. I don't want to immerse the Court too deeply in the complicated logistics of scheduling, but I wanted to pass on a discussion I had with Mr. Robinson and the anticipated scheduling so that the Court would be aware and we have a reasonable degree of certainty. We don't anticipate, as I think the Court would have expected, that we will have another witness on the stand this week. With respect to Monday, because one of the witnesses has some intra-European travel commitments, we would reverse the order of the witnesses. Mr. Manning would appear on Monday, to be followed by Mr. Djurdjevic. We would hope to complete the testimony of both by Tuesday, within the Monday and Tuesday period. Originally they both had commitments that we understood required that testimony be completed, but we have discussed the matter with Mr. Djurdjevic. If necessary, he can -- his testimony can continue on Wednesday, but it needs to be completed by then. So that's why we reversed the order. There's no objection with the Defence and I wanted to alert the Court accordingly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for the information, Mr. Tieger. Yes, please, Mr. Nicholls, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Still just a few more questions on this meeting, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go to page -- if I could have the document back up, this is 22049 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's on Sanction. Let's go to e-court, switch it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Ah, thank you. Could I have page 63 of the English, which I -- which should be 57 -- 56, excuse me, of the Serbian. Now, the English is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: General Milovanovic, on your version, do you see your response there that we were talking about to Mr. Krajisnik, where you explained to him that you had an order from General Mladic regarding this convoy or these buses of men?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that part, but I don't understand what the question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I haven't asked the question yet, General. And I just wanted to confirm that this was the part that you were talking about before the break, where you said you responded and explained that we have the correct section here. Is that the correct part, General?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's my conversation. It wasn't a response. You have responses in parliaments, but within the Supreme Command you have discussions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I'm not sure that the English version is identical to the Serbian. There's Gvero, Karadzic, Milovanovic, and here we have -- oh, yes, General Milanovic is at the top.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Milovanovic, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. Could we now go over to page 65 of the English, which should be at page 58 in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I'm interested in the part where Mr. Karadzic speaks now. And he says, and we talked about this when we met a few weeks ago: "It is the standpoint of our policy. There has been a separation of peoples, of cultures, of worlds. What Vojkan did is not allowed, for Vojkan too worked illegally" --

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm looking at page number 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, this should be page 58, the e-court number in the Serbian, if my page numbers are correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I think it's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, it's marked page 17 on the top, General, but we have different page numbers in our electronic system. I'll read the part and see if you can find it. "What Vojkan did is not allowed, for Vojkan too worked illegally. He was excluded from the state commission, et cetera. What do private agencies do, they find, probably for big money, they secure him a foreign visa and secure him a passport to travel to that foreign country. What happens now, if that were being done by a state institution, we would be accused of ethnic cleansing. A private arrangement between a Muslim and a private firm is absolutely none of our business, absolutely none of our business, and of the 100 Muslims who go to Europe, only ten will come back. There is no patriotism in them. They are simply looking to take to their heels." Now, were you able to find that part, General?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And we can see that here. This is after Mr. Krajisnik spoke. What did you as a member of the Main Staff at the Supreme Command meeting, what did you understand Mr. Karadzic to be saying there?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be read out to the end, please, so that we can understand it correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think -- yes, General, could you read out -- no, read this entire paragraph yourself and ... Let us know if you are done with the reading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read through to the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you answer my question, General? Do you remember it?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. You were here at the Supreme Command session. Mr. -- President Karadzic has spoken just after General -- after Mr. Krajisnik about this issue of freedom of movement and the buses. What did you understand here that General -- that President Karadzic was saying to you on this issue?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, do I have to answer this question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow your comment. Do you have difficulty in answering this question? What is your understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the question is how I understood this, but I'm asking you to tell me whether I have to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, if you could.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I'll answer it. In the course of this discussion of Mr. Karadzic's, I came to the conclusion that he as the president of the republic also knew that this was being done in Republika Srpska. And previously in my discussion it says that I at the time of the session, I found out that this was being done for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what was being done? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean that there were Muslims and Croats who were being taken over the state border and this was being privately organised. The state border is a state institution, and therefore it's impossible to do something that involves the state border and have the state organs remain ignorant of the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I'll just ask this. From this discussion Mr. Krajisnik's view, that "none of us would shed a tear" if they left, that we saw; and President Karadzic saying, If we did this, we would be accused of ethnic cleansing, what did you on the Main Staff understand that their view was about Muslims remaining in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it would be better for Mr. Nicholls to quote rather than interpret. This isn't fair to the witness either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness has read the passage. What is your question, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: From the passages we've read from what Mr. Krajisnik said and what Mr. Karadzic said about these private arrangements, what was your understanding - you as a member of the Main Staff - on what Mr. Karadzic's view was of whether it was desirable to have Muslims remain in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I protest. Again, that's not what the passage says, and this question can't be put on the basis of this passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Well, he didn't cite specific passage. He referred to the entire passage the General had read, and the question was: What was his understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This passage, how he understood, this passage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and this is distorting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you can take up the issue in your cross-examination, but at this time please don't intervene -- interrupt Mr. Nicholls' question. General Milovanovic, do you remember the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My opinion on this discussion of Mr. Karadzic's at the session of the Supreme Command was asked for, and as a representative of the Main Staff -- well, I wasn't the representative of the Main Staff at that session. I had the commander of the Main Staff next to me at that session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably you need to repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll ask you again, General, and again the reason I'm asking you this is because it's something we talked about before and you -- how did you take these comments by Mr. Karadzic? I didn't say you were there as the representative of the Main Staff, but you were on the Main Staff at this time and the supreme commander is talking to you. How did you take these statements regarding Mr. Karadzic's view of whether it was desirable to have Muslims remaining in the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I think this question has been put in a slightly complicated manner. I'll answer the question as I understood it. The first part of the question or the first question is how did I view Mr. Karadzic's statement at the session, his statement that it would be good to have as small as possible number of Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina. My understanding was that this was -- Mr. Karadzic had expressed his own opinion, his private opinion, that there should be very few able-bodied Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I was a bit surprised by this because we both knew that the Muslims going to the territory of Croatia were later returning to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So it was just one stop on the way to their return to Bosnia and Herzegovina. And the second part of the question, well, President Karadzic wasn't expressing something the state wanted. He was expressing what he felt. He thought it would be better for there to be 5.000 less Muslims around Teslic. It would be better if they didn't return to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender this document, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What pages shall we admit?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: My submission would be that it would be good to admit the entire session. It's a verbatim tape-recording, so it -- it doesn't have a -- well, it's minutes so it doesn't have an accuracy problem. The witness has spoken about a few parts of it. I think it's a useful document to have because it's the notes of a Supreme Command session. To go through the entire --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: However, the Chamber's preference is to admit those pages dealt with with the witness in terms of volumes of -- just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, do you have any observation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. President, it seems like this is something akin to like the Assembly sessions that we've admitted in their entirety and perhaps this can be an exception and be admitted in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. -- oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. The Chamber will admit it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit Number P4498.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: One last question about Supreme Command sessions. I speak to you now about your experience from those you attended, General Milovanovic. How would the decisions be made at the end of the sessions, or how would decisions be made? Was there voting or not?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depended. The sessions that I attended weren't sessions where there was the traditional kind of voting that involved raising your hand. I attended sessions without the supreme commander, that was after he signed the Vance-Owen Plan on the 2nd of May, 1993 or 1994. When the members of the Supreme Command would express their opinions about that signature, well, Momcilo Krajisnik was chairing the session and I was asked to express my opinion. I didn't experience a session of the Supreme Command where there was majority voting, or rather, where the participants had to vote by raising their hands. There were discussions, explanations, people tried to convince each other, and then usually the supreme commander would adopt conclusions and tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, one of the things we talked about earlier and we talked about that in terms of some of the orders is whether they would go directly sometimes from President Karadzic to the corps. What I want to ask you about now is just briefly about the situation in Sarajevo. And can you tell us whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, we are leaving this Supreme Command session?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was it 31st March?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's the 31st of March, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And was it the day on which directive 7/1 was issued, General Milovanovic? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the directive was not mentioned at the session at that day at all. As we saw this morning, it was issued on the 8th of March, 1995, that is to say, 23 days before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I meant directive 7/1. Mr. Nicholls, could you give the exhibit number for 7/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, it's P02246, and you are correct, Your Honour, it's the same date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You don't remember that, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Were you involved in issuing directive 7/1? Did you put that question, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I did not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not involved in issuing directive 7/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you didn't read directive 7/1 at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I read it only about ten years later when I read directive number 7. We discussed that when I testified the first time the end of May 2007, here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So not only directive 7 but also 7/1, you read them only in 2007, both of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask you now briefly - and this is something else not related to directive 7/1 - if you could tell us about President Karadzic's relationship to the Sarajevo Corps commanders, whether in the Main Staff there was a feeling that he had a special relationship with General Galic or General Milosevic that may have caused any problems in the command chain.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The system of command in the chain from the Supreme Command Main Staff to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was the same as it was in relation to other corps. However, when the previous head of staff, Colonel Dragan Macetic [phoen], was replaced, Colonel Milosevic was brought in as Chief of Staff of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Sometime in December or, to be more specific, on the 10th of December, 1993, President Karadzic invited me to come for a talk. It was a preparation for the departure of a military political delegation of Republika Srpska to attend a meeting in Belgrade that had been scheduled for the 13th of December. He told me what the agenda would be in Belgrade and he said that it was General Mladic; General Milovanovic; Colonel Milosevic, as Chief of Staff; and a brigade commander, Dragan Josipovic, who would be on this delegation. Dragan Josipovic was commander of the 3rd Brigade of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. I told him straight away that it would not be a good thing for the Chief of Staff to go, since there was a corps commander, General Galic, whereas Lieutenant-Colonel Josipovic as a brigade commander had no place in these talks at strategic level. Upon my return to the Main Staff, I familiarised General Mladic with the subject of my meeting with the supreme commander, and Mladic thought that these two men should not go. I met him again on the 12th of December after the meeting I had with the Chief of Staff of UNPROFOR for BH, I think it was General Ramsey. I told President Karadzic what the reaction was of the Main Staff to our conversation held on the 10th of December and that General Mladic also did not agree with these two going. The supreme commander then changed his decision and excluded Milosevic and Josipovic, and he put the corps commander, General Galic, into the delegation. Of course, being a human being, I wondered why Milosevic had been given that kind of priority. I did not get to any kind of conclusion except for the possibility of Milosevic being favoured in relation to corps commander. However, already the following year Galic was pensioned off and Milosevic took over. That was it. I don't have a specific opinion. It's just that personally as Chief of Staff, Chief of Main Staff, I was bothered by this, why the Chief of Staff was to take part in some talks and negotiations, since the commander was there already. Mladic was taking me along so that I would take minutes or whatever, and Galic should have taken Milosevic as well. So it was simply a lack of observance of the military principle of military subordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I don't have any further questions right now, General. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Yes, now, Mr. Karadzic, now it's your turn to cross-examine General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General. Good afternoon to all. I've already greeted Their Excellencies at the very outset. Have you received interpretation, General?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I keep receiving interpretation all the time. Well, yes, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, let's start with the most recent part. Some mistakes of mine, as you consider them, were referred to just now. Do you agree that I accepted quite a few suggestions, in that case and in other cases, and there were no negative consequences to be suffered by anyone who criticised me in any way; right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably you will be aware by now, General, could you please put a pause between the question and the answer for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I know that. I think that I abided by that over these past two days, but now I just blurted it out. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is because we both speak Serbian, and before you had to wait for the interpretation of Mr. Nicholls' words.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we are starting with the most recent bit, can we go back to P4497. Let us try to understand properly the last paragraph that we saw on our screens. P4498, in Serbian 58, e-court, and in English it's page 65. In Serbian 58, in English 65.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, please take a look at this briefly. What was the plan that Muratovic presented to Krajisnik? He said that the eastern part from Brcko would be taken by them and so on; however, this part that pertains to my view, that it's good -- or rather, that it's not good for them to be there and that they would not return. What is written here, General? Does it say here that my return -- that my concern has to do with their return to fighting? He would go to Travnik and I hope that not more than 10 per cent would return. Does that mean returning for combat purposes or returning ever?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't really know what you're asking me now. Do you want me to confirm what is written here? "Out of 100 Muslims who go to Europe, only ten will come back"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And please go on. So what is my concern, whether they would go back to fight or whether they would go to a third country? Do you see Travnik here. If he were a patriot, he would go back to Travnik, he would not go to third countries; right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, but I don't see what you want me to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. I'll try to simplify it. Mr. Nicholls suggested that I did not wish to have Muslims in Bosnia or Republika Srpska. Please take a look at this, how this was presented and interpreted, the example of Teslic. What is it that I'm saying here, that we had to say that Muslims from Teslic from the front line should be pulled into the territory in depth, that we guard them as civilians so that they do not fall victim?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you said this. That is written faithfully as far as I can remember what you said. I don't see why I would be analysing your words. I can only help you with this, that you gave a very high percentage of return, that is, 10 per cent. I cannot change anything here in the text. That is what was said. My understanding of these words of yours was as follows. This was an explanation as to why it was a good thing for private groups to work on the moving out of Muslims so that the state would not be involved. I don't understand what it is that you want me to confirm or deny.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. First of all this, General, bringing the Muslims in, into the territory, as an attack was expected to take place on Teslic, was that ethnic cleansing or was this a measure that was envisaged by our laws?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If pulling them into the territory in depth, as you said here, if that is protection of the civilian population, then that is a positive measure; that is not ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And these thoughts of mine regarding return, does that have to do with returning to fighting in times of combat? Please take a look at the rest of that sentence.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you say here is that somewhere at some point in time you asked the Main Staff -- well, where labour brigades were necessary, put them to work. They have to work too. I don't remember that request of yours. Perhaps you addressed it to General Mladic. But as far as I know, the army, or rather, the Main Staff never asked for Muslim work units. There were Muslim work units in smaller towns, specifically I know near Gradiska there is a Muslim village, Dubrave. Able-bodied men of military age who did not want to go into the so-called Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and who did not want to join the Army of Republika Srpska, nor did they have to, they made up a work unit that maintained that farm near Gradiska. I'm not aware of any massive use of Muslims in work units as they did in Sarajevo when they used Serbs for these work units that fortified positions around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I meant the upper part of the paragraph. Who will return, how many Muslims. Is it not clear here that I'm concerned how many of them will return and go back to fighting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of this sentence and this, out of 100 Muslims who go to Europe, only ten will return, I don't know whether you meant the entire population that would go to Europe, and out of them 10 per cent would return. Or did you mean able-bodied men. I cannot see that from this document and I'm not capable of seeing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's have a look at how this discussion with Mr. Krajisnik ended and how he understood something he was not aware of previously. It's at the bottom of the page. It says, I don't think General Milovanovic said anything that was false, but there are some things that have to be clarified now. First of all, I had no idea about a convoy of any kind nor did I know that people would be going nor who was exporting them. Rajko Kasagic called me, he says. Our policy is such as stated by President Karadzic, and I think that we all want that, not to ethnically cleanse them. And then it mentions freedom of movement and so on and so forth. And further down, it says ethnic cleansing is a big problem. So in a certain sense this misunderstanding was cleared up. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I think it's clear to both of us that at this session Momcilo Krajisnik bit his tongue. He also wanted me to be placed in the category of generals who had been attacked and I'm grateful to him for that. However, he explained this in a manner that did him no good. He discovered the existence of groups that were making private arrangements to move people out. So he cannot now deny what I said. In a certain sense he praised me, he accepted the fact that I was telling the truth. So I was no longer considered responsible for not having carried out state obligations, as he said, obligations given to me from the state organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I have to put questions in a way that will enable you to answer by saying yes or no, but you can expand whenever you like. So he understood something that he hadn't understood at the time that he was angry; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it clear that these private agencies cannot force the Muslims to leave, but they pay them -- for them to obtain visas and they pay for the trip and for the service?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't agree with that because here information is provided according to which this was done for 6.000 German marks per person. Who did that money go to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see page 25 in the document. It's page 28 in the English version, page 25 in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's have a look at the line that starts with "freedom of movement." It's somewhere halfway down the page. Have you found that part? Yes, you can see where the cursor is now. It says: "The freedom of movement is allowed with the intention of us getting as many Serbs as possible out from the Muslim part of the territory, and if the Muslims want to leave our territory, we should make this possible for them without the use of force because we don't have the right to do that and no one should undertake ethnic cleansing." Is that what Mr. Krajisnik said at the session? And do you remember that we were always trying to get Serbs out of Sarajevo and Tuzla and our idea of freedom of movement was to get Serbs out. It wasn't a matter of driving the Muslims out.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the time that has passed, I cannot now remember whether this is what Krajisnik said, but I have no reason not to believe the transcript and the transcript says that that's what he said. However, I'm assisting you in the following manner today. I said that -- well, when we started discussing this subject matter I said that Alija Izetbegovic wouldn't allow people to leave big towns, Sarajevo, Tuzla, and I don't know which other towns I mentioned. So this sentence here, freedom of movement is allowed with the objective of us getting as many Serbs out of the Muslim part of the territory, well, that's fine and that tallies with the policies pursued by Republika Srpska. The army couldn't ask itself whether it would do this or not. It had to strive to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 62 you said that Muslims were prohibited from leaving Sarajevo, Tuzla, and Srebrenica. But you didn't say who introduced this ban. Can we agree that this ban on the movement of civilians, Muslims and Serbs, was a ban issued by the Serbian --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: By the Muslim authorities, not by us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A minute ago you said that the Muslim able-bodied men didn't have to and they on the whole didn't want to join the VRS. Do we agree that the obligation for mobilisation and for recruitment only concerned Serbs and everyone else was free to act as they saw fit. Do we agree that this was a form of positive discrimination?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, apart from positive discrimination, discrimination is discrimination whether it's positive or not. Of course it was a matter of their own free will. If they wanted to join the VRS, they could do so. And we had a battalion that was called the Mesa Selimovic Battalion, and its members were exclusively of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to a fresh subject, the fresh subject directive number 7 -- directive number 4. Could we see 65 ter number 4315 and let's have a look at this document. It's an analysis on the conduct of combat operations under the code-name Breakthrough, where directives 4 and 5 are implemented within the framework of this operation, the code-name of which is Breakthrough. And could I ask you to have a look at the documents that are referred to, the combat documents on the basis of which this operation was carried out. Have a look at the bottom. The operation Proboj starts on the 24th of November. Do we agree that that is the date on which General Zivanovic issued the combat order that we have had a look at and which to a certain extent amended what was said in directive 4?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we scroll up a bit and zoom in. The letters are too small.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I can be of assistance, it mentions directive number 4, amendments --

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Decision on liberating Konjevic Polje and so on. And then does it say that the co-ordination group, the group for co-ordinating the activities, consisted of Colonel Miladin Prstojevic and the others -- Colonel Miladin Prstojevic and the others; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's have a look at the second page, please. Under (b) it says at the beginning of operation, and then it mentions the enemy forces, its deployment in the wider Skelani sector, and at the bottom at the end it says -- can we scroll up. It says Bratunac-Skelani were defended in the operation and the enemy attack was repelled and so on and so forth. Do we agree about that, and then let's go back to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we scroll up a bit so that I can see the rest. Yes, I've seen that. And what is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's have a look at the first page. Do we agree that a decision was taken on liberating Pobudje, Konjevic Polje, and Cerska on the 8th of December -- yes, the third bullet, third line under (b). It has to do with the liberation of Pobudje, the 8th of December, 1992, and Miladin Prstojevic -- Colonel Miladina Prstojevic is appointed as the chief of purposes for co-ordination. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miladin Prstojevic, Colonel Miladin Prstojevic, was an operations officer at the time in the corps command. However, if I may add something about this operation, Breakthrough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead if there's anything you believe is relevant, you can tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the usual names for military operations are geographical terms, Podrinje 93, Corridor 92, for example, or Lukavac, the village of Lukavac, 93. The General, or rather, Colonel Zivanovic at the time was obsessed with certain other terms because -- other names because this operation, Breakthrough Operation, it wasn't an operation in the operative sense of the term. This is a battle liberating a village. Kamenica can't be a matter of combat. Two or three brigades are involved in combat, in a battle. But to liberate Kamenica perhaps one battalion would be sufficient or perhaps a brigade. That's a fight. So these are minor operations. These are fights and battles organised by the Drina Corps. And he would give them these names, such as Breakthrough. We mentioned the Operation Pesnica, or Fist, today. So these were unusual terms. These were names used for brief operations. For example, Operation Fist. You hit someone with your fist, if you break his head, fine; if not, fine. And that was the case with Operation Breakthrough. He received a task in accordance with directive 4. The task was to defend the towns in Podrinje - I won't list the names of the towns - and he was to use other forces to exhaust the enemy and to inflict losses on the enemy, and that takes us back to directive number 4. So the Birac territory was to be left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document be admitted and then we'll have a look at the decision on liberating Pobudje and Konjevic Polje. Your Excellency, could this document please be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be next Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2135, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are with this document. Mr. Nicholls, do you see the first paragraph? It refers to the amendment of the directive dated 25th of November, and also amended directive amended 7th of December. Do we have that in our evidence or do you have that in your custody?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I believe so, Your Honour. We have -- I'll check. We have the -- I'm having difficulty seeing it now on the screen. -- yeah, for sure the 7 December 1992 and I'll have to check on the first one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. If the Chamber could see them. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. On the 7th of December there was an amendment to directive 4. Could we see 65 ter document 9148 issued on the 8th of December, an order on liberation of these villages. 95 [as interpreted] ter 9148, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please have a look. Above all, do we agree that it's not referring to directive 4, and under item 1, as usual, the enemy is described. Isn't that correct? And 10- to 15.000 armed soldiers are identified in the Srebrenica-Zepa-Cerska sectors and Kamenica as well towards Zvornik. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 2 it says what sort of weapons the enemy has, but could we have a look at the last page. Do we agree that in the first two lines the co-ordination group is named and Miladin Prstojevic is the person first mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is in evidence as Exhibit D1597.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Can we now have 65 ter 2542.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us see what Mr. Prstojevic, who was appointed by General Zivanovic -- I mean, let us see what his position is and how he's going to act and co-ordinate. The 18th of December, 1992, isn't that right? It says "urgent." And what he's writing is information on the need to adhere to international norms in war. So the order is to be implemented by way of this information on the need to adhere to international norms in war; right? Actually, I'm asking you to read the first page. In line 3, there's a reference to wounded persons, civilians, humane qualities and so on. And towards the end of the paragraph it says that we should prevent any kind of abuse on our side. A bit further down it says that we must bear in mind that for a state to be internationally recognised it must first and foremost be a state based on rule of law. And then it says what that means. If you've read it, you can ask for the next page.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read the document only a few days ago, two or three days ago, either when I saw you or when I saw the Prosecutor, so we can move on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the next page. Yes, here it is. Do we agree, General, that here on this page it is not only that he's issuing an order. He is also appealing, beseeching, saying that humaneness is so important. In line two, four, six, eight from the top, he says when there is violence the most important thing is to be humane and so on and so forth. Do we agree that this is considerable care on the part of this officer, who is in charge of co-ordinating the operation?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. This is an attempt made by Colonel Prstojevic to act as a shock absorber for the first sentence of Zivanovic's order that has to do with treatment of the civilian population. Colonel Miladin Prstojevic worked in the Main Staff. When the Drina Corps was established, as you know yourself, I brought Colonel Zivanovic for a meeting with you on the 15th of January, 1993. In the corps they did not really write very well, so we were trying to find a way out. First of all, there were personnel mistakes made by Mladic appointing Zivanovic corps commander. He appointed him corps commander as a kind of reward for the fact that he had been wounded. This is a man who still has 21 bullets in his body. When Mladic made that decision when visiting him at the JNA and I said, "For heaven's sake, boss, how can Zivanovic command a corps? He's a good artillery man." And Mladic said, "Well, that's what I thought, but you and I will go on commanding the corps." Then I took Prstojevic out of the Main Staff because I knew him very well and I sent him there to be operations officer in the corps command to make them more literate, if you will, and you see what the man is doing. He cannot annul the corps commander's order, but he's diluting it, he's explaining to people what war crimes are and basically he's explaining international law and the law of war. He was not doing this as a matter of capriciousness or because he was bored and didn't have enough work. He was precisely doing it for the purpose that you referring to and that is preventing mistreatment of the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Was this officer ever punished on account of this or was he promoted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the 25 -- sorry to interrupt. The 25 November 1992 addition to operative directive number 4 is 65 ter 09348, so we do have that. The 7 December 1992 order to amend directive number 4 is in evidence as P4249.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, this is what I wanted to ask: This kind of action taken by Colonel Prstojevic, did it harm him or did -- was it a recommendation? Did this recommend him as a good officer? Was he punished for explaining the order in this way?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to speak openly. Because of such actions, Colonel Prstojevic was persecuted by the corps commander. Now, was it after this -- but at any rate, while he was operations officer in the corps command, he was there for a brief period of time only, he came to see me at the staff. He was upset, he was angry, and he said to me, "Send me anywhere, just as far away as possible from Zivanovic. I cannot take it." I think that I returned him to the Main Staff again, to the teaching sector with Miletic. And after General Spremo was retired as Chief of Staff of the Sarajevo Corps, Prstojevic was appointed -- sorry, it was the Herzegovina Corps actually. And then he was appointed Chief of Staff and he became a general there and he retired as a general of the Army of Republika Srpska. We were aware of the clashes between him and General Zivanovic, just as later there would be a conflict between General Zivanovic and Vinko Pandurevic, who was then a rising officer. Then also his Chief of Staff, General Krstic. I mean, Zivanovic could not take any kind of objections. He always relied on the commander of the Main Staff because he had brought him there in the first place from the Knin Corps, or rather, from the Benkovac garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. However, may we conclude by saying that in the Main Staff, Prstojevic was not being stopped. So even if not being favoured, at least he was promoted on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the beginning of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because it was the Main Staff, not corps commands, that pursued personnel policy in the army. So these conflicts between Zivanovic as corps commander and his subordinates did not affect the career of his subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2136, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 15307, could we please take a look at that, unless it's already been admitted on some basis. I mean, even if it has been admitted, let's have a look at it, 65 ter number 15307.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree, General, that at the time until the liberation of Cerska and Konjevic Polje, this was a single Muslim military space from Zepa, including Kamenica, Zepa, Srebrenica, a large part of the municipality of Bratunac, a part of the Milici municipality; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You don't have English translation, do you, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] English? I don't know. I see that this question has been recorded in the transcript and I hear you. I hear the interpretation of what you're saying into Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now there's a question for you, General. Until spring 1993, is it true that this was a single --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, my question is whether we have English translation of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I suppose so, 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that that was mentioned today, this operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Reid has found a translation and is uploading it for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, do we agree that what is described here is Operation Pesnica, Fist, that was carried out between the 11th of January, 1993, until the 20th of January, 1993, after Operation Proboj, Breakthrough; right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.
